column1: # Linux file capabilities: what each one actually grants.
# See capabilities(7). severity is what a file carrying this capability scores by default.

column3: description
Set any user id, including 0. On an interpreter this is a root shell in one line.
Set any group id, including groups that own sensitive files.
Set file capabilities on any file, so it can grant itself every other capability.
Bypass all read and directory-search permission checks. Reads /etc/shadow and every key on the box.
Bypass all read, write and execute permission checks. Effectively full filesystem control.
Bypass ownership checks on chmod, chown and friends.
Change the ownership of any file.
The catch-all capability: mount, namespaces, device control. Treat it as root.
Load and unload kernel modules. Kernel code execution, game over.
Attach to any process, including root ones, and inject code into them.
Raw I/O port and /dev/mem access. Read and rewrite kernel memory.
Change the MAC (SELinux/AppArmor) policy.
Ignore the MAC policy entirely.
Create device nodes - make a raw disk device and read the filesystem around permissions.
Reboot the machine or load a new kernel with kexec.
Call chroot, which is an escape primitive when combined with other capabilities.
Override resource limits, including reserved filesystem space and kernel queues.
Set the system clock. Breaks logging, certificates and Kerberos.
Send signals to any process regardless of owner.
Reconfigure networking: interfaces, routes, firewall rules, promiscuous mode.
Load BPF programs. Depending on the kernel this reaches a lot of privileged state.
Performance monitoring across the system, which leaks memory contents.
Change the audit subsystem - disable the logging that would record what happens next.
Checkpoint and restore processes, including other users' memory.
Modify the capability sets of processes.
Set and clear the immutable and append-only file attributes.
Bypass permission checks on shared memory and other IPC objects.
Open raw and packet sockets: sniff traffic and forge packets. Normal for ping, tcpdump and mtr.
Read the kernel ring buffer, which leaks addresses useful for defeating KASLR.
Read the audit log.
Write records into the audit log.
Bind to ports below 1024. The normal reason a web server does not need to be root.
Send broadcast and multicast traffic.
Lock memory so it cannot be swapped out. Normal for password and key handling.
Take out file leases.
Change scheduling priority. Normal for audio and real-time tooling.
Turn process accounting on and off.
Configure and hang up terminals.
Set a timer that wakes the system.
Prevent the system from suspending.
Non-standard name; check capabilities(7) for what your kernel calls it.
